A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PPI-NO work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across substantial relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: Section 5 and the appendices report original evaluations of PPI-FNO and PPI-DONet on five PDE benchmarks and fatigue modeling, including ablations and prediction visualizations.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds sequential-pipeline comparisons, distribution-shift and noisy-data experiments, and training-time measurements.

M1.justification: The evaluated surrogate architecture, losses, and alternating procedure in Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. New Section 6.1 proposes adaptations for coefficient, initial-condition, and boundary-condition inputs, including a contrastive residual objective and a boundary-enforcing formulation. These are untested methodological extensions, not demonstrated changes to the benchmark implementation.

E1.justification: The five PDE benchmarks and fatigue-modeling task are retained. Coverage expands within existing benchmarks to shifted input distributions for Advection and Nonlinear Diffusion, and sparse, noisy observations for Nonlinear Diffusion. The more general PDE settings discussed in Section 6.1 are not evaluated.

E2.justification: v2 Table 6 adds SINDy-to-FNO and learned-phi-network-to-FNO sequential pipelines on Darcy Flow and Nonlinear Diffusion. SINDy was previously discussed but not evaluated. Existing FNO, DONet, PI-FNO, and architectural-ablation comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The original benchmark settings are retained, but substantial new protocols are introduced: sequential training with generated data; test kernel length scales of 0.15 versus training 0.25 for Advection and 0.10 versus 0.20 for Nonlinear Diffusion; and subsampling to 400 values, adding 5% Gaussian noise, then Gaussian-process interpolation back to 128-by-128 grids.

E4.justification: Section 5.2 adds tests of sequential versus joint learning, distribution-shift robustness of both the physics surrogate and PPI-FNO, sparse/noisy-data robustness, and training-time overhead. These substantially extend the existing architecture, derivative-order, loss-weight, learning-curve, and rich-data analyses, which are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five evaluations with randomly resampled training sets and report means with standard deviations. Additional result tables continue that reporting style. The new discussion of correlated grid samples and effective sample size introduces no corresponding uncertainty estimator, significance test, or revised repetition count.

E6.justification: All eight v1 tables retain their numerical entries in corresponding v2 tables. New Tables 6, 9, 10, 12, and 13 add pipeline, robustness, and timing results. For example, shifted Advection with 80 examples gives errors of 0.6471 for PPI-FNO and 0.6484 for FNO; noisy Nonlinear Diffusion with 30 examples gives 0.0504 and 0.0606, respectively.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 adds finite-difference error and grid-size scaling, universal-approximation arguments, and VC-dimension/sample-complexity statements. Section 6.1 adds generalized PDE formulations and reasoning about avoiding a trivial zero residual through a contrastive objective. The original mathematical formulation remains, without a new PPI-NO-specific convergence or generalization proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and central conclusion retain the same claims: learning pseudo physics from limited data improves operator learning without requiring known governing equations. The novelty claim and five-benchmark-plus-fatigue scope remain. The initial-condition caveat added to the conclusion already appeared in v1 Appendix C.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands limitations concerning difficult multiscale PDEs, spurious learned relationships, correlated grid samples, resolution dependence, and the distinction between predictive surrogates and discovered physical laws. It also interprets the new sequential-pipeline, robustness, and timing results and clarifies that residual regularization does not supply additional labeled pairs.

D1.justification: v2 adds an implementation-release link, specifies centered finite differences, identifies the RTX 4090 workstation used for timing, and documents the new robustness preprocessing. The extensive original hyperparameter settings are moved from Appendix A.7 into Section 5 without substantive changes. Table 12 reports runtime values but does not specify their units.

R1.justification: Five references are added for approximation theory, finite differences, learning theory, and PixelCNN. The new SINDy comparison further develops the distinction between explicit equation identification and flexible learned PDE representations. The principal positioning relative to neural operators, PINO, and cycle consistency remains.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is reorganized into predictive-performance and ablation subsections. Hyperparameters and pointwise-error analysis move from the appendices into the main text, alongside a substantial new Discussions and Limitations section. Core introductory passages remain largely intact, but the document structure and explanatory treatment change extensively.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a two-column conference layout to a single-column journal layout, with extensive relocation and resizing of tables and figures. Panels from v1 Figures 3 and 6 are regrouped into v2 Figures 8 and 9. Five new tables and two new distribution-shift heatmap figures supplement the retained displays.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps through sequential-pipeline comparisons, distribution-shift and noisy-data tests, and measured computational overhead. These expose both persistent benefits and sharply reduced gains under harder conditions. The expanded limitations substantially improve interpretation of the unchanged main results. Although the proposed general-PDE extensions remain unvalidated and timing units are missing, the added evidence and qualifications make the method's benefits, costs, and applicability substantially easier to assess.
